# Saṅkhajātaka (Ja 442)

**ID:** Ja 442
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Saṅkhajātaka* (Ja 442) is a canonical birth-story preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its opening frame narrative, the Buddha related the discourse at Jetavana in connection with the lay offering of all monastic requisites. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta is born during the reign of King Brahmadatta in Molinī as the brahmin Saṅkha, a pious householder who dispenses alms daily to beggars and travelers [Law 1931]. Fearing the exhaustion of his charitable wealth, Saṅkha embarks on a maritime voyage to acquire riches, pausing beforehand to render homage and penance to a paccekabuddha [Law 1931]. The narrative serves as a prime exemplum of the Bodhisatta's cultivation of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) [Mein Da 2015].

A hallmark of the jātaka is the seafaring crisis and shipwreck, leading to the miraculous rescue of Saṅkha by the ocean deity Maṇimekhalā, who protects righteous travelers [Law 1931; Monius 2001]. In the *samodhāna* or identification of characters, this guardian deity is identified with the eminent nun Uppalavaṇṇā [Monius 2001]. Saṅkha's encounter with the sea goddess represents a pivotal early depiction of Maṇimekhalā, a figure central to trans-regional Buddhist literature and celebrated prominently in the classical Tamil Buddhist poem *Maṇimēkalai* [Monius 2001; Lewis and Tuladhar 2000].
